title: Determining the Number of Symmetry Sectors in Composite Quantum Spectra
authors: Nisarg Vyas, S. Harshini Tekur, M. S. Santhanam
abstract: The spectral fluctuations in complex quantum systems are modeled in terms of spectra from random matrices. Quantitative agreement with random matrices holds only when the quantum spectrum is a pure sequence, and not a composite spectrum that mixes levels from different symmetry sectors. It was shown earlier that discrete symmetries in composite spectra can be detected using higher-order spacing ratio statistics provided the symmetry sectors are of equal dimensions. The general case is when the symmetry sectors have unequal dimensions, and the symmetries of the Hamiltonian system are unknown or only partially known. In this work, we address how the number of symmetry sectors can be determined from a composite spectrum arising in Hermitian and non-Hermitian settings. A Best Subset Technique is proposed for determining the number of the symmetry sectors by comparing the spectral fluctuations to that of an appropriate random matrix ensemble without requiring de-symmetrization. It is demonstrated using spectra from Gaussian, Wishart and Ginibre ensembles, and also for spectra drawn from many-body quantum systems.
summary: This paper introduces the Best Subset Technique (BST) to solve the difficult problem of counting symmetry sectors in composite quantum spectra. By analyzing Higher-Order Spacing Ratios on an optimal subset of eigenvalues, the BST can accurately determine the number of contributing symmetry blocks, even when those blocks have unequal dimensions. This method is robustly tested across various random matrix ensembles and physical models.
main_problem: The primary goal is to determine the number of symmetry sectors ($m$) within a composite quantum spectrum when the individual symmetry sectors have unequal dimensions and the underlying symmetries are unknown or only partially known.
main_result: A Best Subset Technique (BST) successfully determines $m$ by analyzing spectral fluctuations, outperforming traditional methods that fail when sector dimensions are unequal.
method: The BST uses Higher-Order Spacing Ratios (HOSRs) and minimizes the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence between the empirical HOSR distribution and expected random matrix ensemble distributions.
model_or_system: The analysis applies to composite spectra derived from Hermitian and non-Hermitian systems, tested using random matrix ensembles like Gaussian, Wishart, and Ginibre matrices, as well as many-body models like the Transverse Field Ising Model (TFIM).
key_observables: Higher-Order Spacing Ratios (HOSRs) and the resulting best-fit parameters ($k^*, f^*$) used in the BST.
important_parameters: The number of symmetry sectors ($m$), the fraction of the spectrum analyzed ($f$), and the order of the ratio ($k$).
main_assumptions: The core assumption is that the HOSRs calculated on a specific, optimal subset (the 'best subset') of the spectrum can reliably proxy the underlying spectral statistics, even when the full spectrum is complex.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the failure of standard HOSR analysis on composite spectra (e.g., four GUE matrices) and demonstrate the success of the BST in correctly deducing the number of blocks ($m=4$ or $m=3$) by analyzing specific spectral fractions.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem of composite spectra, details the HOSR formalism, proposes the BST using KL divergence minimization, and validates the technique by applying it successfully to multiple random matrix ensembles (Gaussian, Wishart, Ginibre) and physical models (TFIM).
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful, general diagnostic tool for analyzing complex quantum spectra, which is crucial for understanding spectral rigidity and symmetry breaking in disordered or interacting quantum systems.
